messages.content: Identify all predictive claims made in August 2026 regarding short term BDI movements (30 day horizon), by conviction and consensus vs disagreement between analysts. Test these claims against September data.

The full analysis is in the report. Summary:

**August 2026 forecasts (30-day horizon) — consensus vs. disagreement**
- **Consensus (high conviction):** no major downward correction, Capesize-led strength sustained by vessel-supply tightness. Breakwave (4 & 18 Aug), BIMCO SMOO, and late-August broker notes were aligned.
- **Disagreement:** (1) Signal Group's supply/demand forward-balance model predicted C3/C5 supply surplus to widen into early September (easing) — the explicit bearish near-term call; (2) Xinde and Breakwave's own China-iron-ore caveat questioned sustainability; (3) no one forecast the breakout magnitude.

**Testing against September data (to 9 Sep)**
- BDI: 2,815 (18 Aug) → 3,620 (9 Sep), +28.6%; first week of September alone +13.9% to a near-5-year high (3,628 on 4 Sep); BCI +20.4% to 6,427.
- **Breakwave "no-correction"** — vindicated (high-conviction claim was right in substance, though "uneventful summer" understated the rally).
- **Signal model (easing into September)** — wrong direction; C3 hit a multi-year high at $41.55/mt and C5 strengthened to high-$18s.
- **Xinde/BIMCO sustainability skepticism** — not falsified medium-term, but the 30-day bearish implication did not materialize; Black Sea grains weakness (Xclusiv) was segment-correct but swamped by Capesize strength.

Sources: OilPriceAPI Baltic reprints [1][2], Breakwave Aug 4 [3] and Aug 18 [4] reports, Signal Week 31/32 forward balances [5][6], Xinde [8], BIMCO [9], SmartShipbroking Week 35 [10], Baird Baltic close [11].

artifacts.title: Bi-Weekly Industry Report
artifacts.subtitle: Broker PDF

highlights: • Steady Demand and Shrinking Vessel Supply Pushes Spot Higher – During the second half of August, robust iron ore transportation demand in the Pacific, driven by all three mining majors, combined with localized storm disruptions that tightened vessel lineups led to elevated freight rates on the critical Australia-to China route. Concurrently, a constricted Atlantic tonnage list pushed spot rates upward despite softer regional demand, positioning the market advantageously from a higher absolute baseline as it transitions out of the historically quiet summer August month and into the seasonally strong autumn period. Additionally, metallurgical coal import demand jumped, following a major accident in China with traders scrambling to secure tonnage of medium-size bulkers. While other maritime segments like tankers and containers are earning significantly higher daily rates, this parallel success has bolstered shipowner sentiment despite any direct fundamental link amongst those segments, potentially amplifying upward spot rate pressure should an unexpected market tightening occur. Consequently, despite generally flat underlying fundamentals in our view, the near-term outlook for spot Capesize rates remains highly optimistic, sustained by a volatile global logistics landscape that continues to drive exceptional volatility and historic performance across the broader shipping industry during a year for global shipping that will be remembered for decades to come.

• Our Long-term View – The last few years have been characterized by increased geopolitical uncertainty. Going forward, we expect such events to continue to affect global trade and have a meaningful impact on effective vessel supply. Combined with the potential for a multi-year cyclical rebound in China’s economic activity following the recent economic turmoil, dry bulk shipping should experience higher volatility on top of a secular tightness driven by stable bulk commodity demand and rather steady but elevated fleet growth.

The Baltic Dry Index (BDI) measures the average spot rates for dry bulk freight with a sector weighting of 40% Capesize, 30% Panamax and 30% Supramax. The Breakwave Dry Futures Index (BDRYFF) is designed to track freight futures contracts with a sector weighting of 50% Capesize, 40% Panamax and 10% Supramax and a weighted average maturity of approximately 50-70 days.

artifacts.title: Signal Weekly Dry Market Monitor: Week 35, 2026
artifacts.subtitle: Ajot

highlights: The BDI rose to 3,186 (+79 day-on-day, +345 WoW) on a stronger week for the larger sizes. Capesize led the increase, with the BCI rising to 5,336 (+784 WoW) and average C5TC earnings climbing to $44,896/day (+$7,111 WoW). Panamax also strengthened, with the BPI rising to 2,315 (+212 WoW) and the P5TC average up to $20,834/day (+$1,906 WoW). The geared sizes were steady: Supramax was flat (BSI 1,647, +7 WoW) and Handysize unchanged on the day (BHSI 881, +7 WoW).

Supply/demand by route. C3 (Tubarao–Qingdao) shows cumulative supply remaining below expected demand throughout the forward window, with the shortfall widening after day 30. On C5 (West Australia–Qingdao), supply initially exceeds expected demand before moving below it from around day 7. Total supply rises above demand again after day 13, but supply excluding laden vessels levels off at approximately 150 vessels and remains in deficit.

Demand-to-supply ratio. C5TC rose 5.6% on the week to $43,024/day in the week ending 27 August, placing C5TC earnings in the 88th percentile of weekly observations over the past year. The demand index stood at 101.72 versus 98.25 for supply, both relative to year-ago levels. This lowered the demand-to-supply ratio to 1.04 from 1.12 in the previous week. The reading remains above 1.00, indicating that demand growth is running slightly ahead of supply growth, but Capesize is not reported as a settled change of side: whether a reading sits above or below the balance point can turn on revision alone, and the range these weekly values move on revision rests on a single vintage pair of six provisional observations.

artifacts.title: TSG - Weekly Dry Market Monitor: Week 31, 2026
artifacts.subtitle: Thesignalgroup

highlights: Driven by a robust performance in the Capesize sector that offset softer results in the Supramax and Handysize segments, the BDI dipped slightly by 11 points to 2,732 (+59 day-on-day, −11 WoW). Specifically, Capesize continued its upward trend, pushing the BCI up to 4,564 (+268 day-on-day, +364 WoW) and boosting average C5TC earnings to around $37,892/day (+$3,305 WoW). The Panamax market also showed strength, with the BPI firming to 2,087 (+47 day-on-day, +63 WoW). In contrast, Supramax proved to be the week's main underperformer, sliding to 1,609 (−1 day-on-day, −85 WoW), while Handysize also lost ground, easing to 887 (−3 day-on-day, −18 WoW).

Supply / Demand - the forward read: As of 31 July 2026, expected demand on C3 (Tubarão–Qingdao) remains above projected vessel supply through most of August. The two curves converge around 27–29 August, after which projected supply moves above expected demand and the surplus widens into the first week of September. On C5 (West Australia–Qingdao), projected supply excluding laden vessels remains above expected demand through most of the 15-day window. The curves converge around 12–13 August, but total projected supply rises sharply thereafter and finishes well above expected demand by 15 August.

artifacts.title: The 2026 freight recovery  — Breakwave Advisors
artifacts.subtitle: Breakwaveadvisors

highlights: The dry bulk freight market delivered a considerably stronger performance during the first seven months of 2026, with Baltic Exchange time-charter equivalent earnings improving across all four major vessel segments compared with January–July 2025. The recovery was broad-based rather than dependent on a single vessel class, reflecting stronger cargo volumes, improved fleet utilisation and firmer demand across both major and minor bulk trades.

Based on the available daily assessments, the Capesize 5TC averaged approximately USD 30,400/day, up 81% from USD 16,800/day during the corresponding period of 2025. Capesize earnings reached a high of USD 46,538/day in late May, while the market closed July at USD 35,457/day, well above the USD 26,858/day recorded at the end of July last year. The improvement extended across the smaller segments. Kamsarmax earnings averaged around USD 17,600/day, increasing 53% year-on-year from USD 11,500/day, while the Ultramax 11TC rose by 48% also near to USD 17,600/day. Handysize earnings recorded the smallest, but still substantial, increase, averaging USD 14,100/day compared with USD 10,100/day in 2025, representing growth of 39%. The progression of rates was also important.

Following a relatively stable opening quarter, earnings strengthened sharply during April and May, particularly for Capesizes and Kamsarmaxes. Ultramax and Handysize markets advanced more steadily, reaching their strongest levels during June and July and demonstrating healthier underlying support across geographically diversified trades. This stronger freight environment was accompanied by an increase in total seaborne dry bulk volumes. Based on the Signal Ocean data, approximately 3.41 billion tonnes were transported during January–July 2026, compared with 3.35 billion tonnes during the same period of 2025, representing growth of almost 2%. Capesize-carried cargo increased by 4.8% to 936.7 million tonnes, lifting its share of total trade from 26.7% to 27.4%. Panamax, Supramax and Handymax volumes also increased, while VLOC, Handysize and Small vessel cargoes declined. The figures therefore indicate that trade growth was concentrated mainly in the larger and medium-sized vessel categories, supporting the segments that experienced the strongest freight improvement.

highlights: ## Bi-Weekly Industry Report August 4, 2026

• Dry Bulk Rate Volatility Collapses as Spot Rates Remain High – The dry bulk market continues to trade at historically elevated levels with no immediate signs of a correction, while freight rate volatility has collapsed to multi-year lows. Current spot rate strength is primarily sustained by structural vessel supply constraints, driven by ongoing geopolitical disruptions and an intensive global drydocking schedule. However, downside risks are accumulating as weakening demand for iron ore in China, the sector's primary trading commodity, threatens to disrupt the market balance. Because freight rates are fundamentally demand-driven and supply enabled, the absence of sustained demand growth is gradually tilting the medium term outlook. While pinpointing the exact catalyst for a market correction remains challenging, investors should look past the current period of price stability, as macroeconomic fundamentals will ultimately drive medium-term freight dynamics. However, shipowners have been riding a very strong market for multiple years in a row and thus maintain extremely healthy cash balances to weather a potential storm, unlike the 2010’ crisis when major companies where forced to reorganize.

artifacts.title: BIMCO Sees Strong Dry Bulk Market in 2026 Despite Strait of Hormuz Risks - India Seatrade News
artifacts.subtitle: Indiaseatradenews

highlights: The global dry bulk shipping market is expected to remain resilient through 2026, supported by stronger cargo demand and longer sailing distances, although the outlook continues to hinge on developments in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the latest market outlook from the BIMCO.

BIMCO has outlined two forecast scenarios based on the future accessibility of the strategic waterway. The first assumes the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed for an extended period, while the second assumes it reopens by the end of the third quarter of 2026. The shipping association noted that the longer the disruption continues, the more closely market conditions will resemble the prolonged closure scenario.

For 2026, BIMCO expects dry bulk fleet supply to grow by 1.5% to 2.5% under both scenarios. Effective supply growth will remain below overall fleet expansion due to increased port congestion and the continued underutilization of approximately 0.5% of the global dry bulk fleet trapped in the Persian Gulf.

Total supply rises above demand again after day 13, but supply excluding laden vessels levels off at approximately 150 vessels and remains in deficit.

artifacts.subtitle: Thesignalgroup

highlights: Capesize remained the primary driver of the market, with the BCI rising to 4,655 (+86 day-on-day, +555 week-on-week), lifting the BDI to 2,944 (+227 WoW). Average C5TC earnings reached approximately $38,711/day. Panamax was almost unchanged on the day, with the BPI at 2,253 (0 day-on-day, +50 WoW), supported by the Pacific round-voyage market. Supramax extended its gradual recovery, with the BSI at 1,706 (+6 day-on-day), while Handysize eased to 915 (-2 day-on-day, -27 WoW), remaining below its recent 52-week highs. Global ballast availability showed small variations across segments, with Panamax, Capesize, and Handysize increasing by 3%, 2%, and 2% week-on-week, respectively, while Supramax ballast declined 2% following the previous week's build-up.

BCI rose to 4,655 (+86 day-on-day; +555 week-on-week), extending the rally that is driving the dry bulk market higher. Average C5TC earnings climbed to $38,711/day (+$780 day-on-day). Iron ore routes firmed further, with C3 (Tubarao–Qingdao) at $33.00/mt and C5 (West Australia–Qingdao) at $13.32/mt, both recovering strongly month-on-month. BCI 52-wk high 5,517 / low 2,104; 5-yr avg 2,728.

On the two iron-ore benchmarks, compared with the previous week, the forward balance on the C3 (Tubarao–Qingdao) has shifted modestly in favour of demand, delaying the point at which cumulative vessel supply overtakes expected demand. For the C5 (West Australia–Qingdao), the forward balance is broadly unchanged. Vessel availability continues to build ahead of expected demand over most of the forward horizon, indicating that the Pacific iron ore market remains more supplied than the Brazil trade.

Global iron ore shipments remained relatively stable in August 2026, according to BigMint. Despite subdued demand from China, the leading producer countries showed mostly positive or neutral trends, with South Africa being the exception.

In the short term, Australian export volumes may be constrained by localized strikes at the key Port of Hedland. Indian sales are expected to recover after the monsoon season, though stricter safety regulations on the east coast could slow ship loading. High-grade Brazilian ore is likely to gain market share as steelmakers seek cost optimization amid high coal prices. South African exports are expected to remain subdued due to ongoing logistical barriers.

artifacts.title: August 2026 BDI Forecasts vs. September Realization
artifacts.subtitle: 30-day predictive claims made in August 2026, tested against the realized BDI/BCI path through 9 September 2026

blocks.text: This note identifies the predictive claims about short-term (≈30-day) BDI movement made during August 2026, grades each by direction and conviction, separates consensus from disagreement, and scores every claim against the realized index path through the latest print (BDI 3,620 on 9 September). Figures are OilPriceAPI reprints of Baltic Exchange assessments unless a broker/report source is cited.

blocks.title: Baltic Dry Index & Capesize Index, Aug 3 – Sep 9 2026
blocks.subtitle: OilPriceAPI reprint of Baltic Exchange assessments

blocks.text: The market bottomed mid-August (BDI 2,776 on 19 Aug), then rose on seven straight sessions into 28 August (3,186), paused on 1 September, and broke out in the first week of September to a near-five-year high (3,628 on 4 Sep) before easing to 3,620. Capesize led throughout: BCI climbed 45% from its 20 August trough (4,429) to 6,427 on 4 September, with C5TC earnings reaching ~$53,508/day in the week to 9 September [1][2][11].
Predictive claims made in August 2026 (30-day horizon)

rows.claim: No immediate signs of a correction; spot rates stay historically elevated
Meaningful downward correction unlikely absent geopolitical resolution; 'uneventful conclusion to summer' then autumn strength
C3 demand above supply through Aug, surplus widens into first week of Sept; C5 in supply surplus from ~12–13 Aug
C3 tips to slight surplus in final ten days; C5 builds surplus from ~day 12 — Capesize easing into late Aug
Black Sea dry-bulk trade in a 'markedly weaker phase' (grains overlay, not headline BDI)
Capesize strength at $30k+/day looks inconsistent with weak China steel demand and 8-yr-low Atlantic netbacks

rows.source: BIMCO SMOO (July 30 edn, in force Aug)
rows.claim: Market 'resilient through 2026'; Hormuz rerouting supports demand; El Niño demand boost; 2027 supply-glut warning
Prompt dry-bulk strength is real, but the forward curve is more cautious (3-week horizon 4–18 Sep)

blocks.text: **Consensus (high agreement).** Every desk active in August shared the same near-term core call: no major downward correction over the following ~30 days, with Capesize-led strength sustained by vessel-supply tightness (geopolitical rerouting across the Black, Red, Arabian and Baltic seas, weather/typhoon dislocations, and heavy drydocking) [3][4][9]. Breakwave (both 4 and 18 August), BIMCO, and the late-August broker notes were directionally aligned on this.

**Disagreement.** Three fault lines separated the field. (1) *Momentum into September* — Signal's supply/demand forward-balance model repeatedly projected the C3/C5 supply surplus to widen into early September (easing pressure), the one explicit bearish near-term call, against a market that surged [5][6]. (2) *Sustainability* — Xinde's 24 August piece, and Breakwave's own China-iron-ore caveat, questioned whether $30k+/day Capesize earnings were consistent with weak Chinese steel demand, elevated port inventories and eight-year-low Atlantic netbacks [3][8]. (3) *Magnitude* — no August source forecast the intensity of the breakout: BDI +13.9% and BCI +20.4% in the first week of September alone, or a fresh five-year high [11]. SmartShipbroking's 'prompt real, forward cautious' note was the closest to hedging on magnitude [10].
Testing the claims against September data

rows.claim: Breakwave (4 Aug): no immediate correction, rates stay elevated
rows.outcome: BDI held >3,000 and rose to 5-yr high 3,628; BCI 6,427

rows.claim: Breakwave (18 Aug): no meaningful correction; 'uneventful' summer then autumn strength
rows.outcome: No correction — right; but BDI +28.6% 18 Aug→9 Sep, first Sep week +13.9% — 'uneventful' magnitude understated

rows.claim: Signal (Wk 31/32): Capesize momentum eases into Sept; C5 soft
rows.outcome: Opposite — C3 to $41.55/mt (multi-yr high), C5 to high-$18s, BCI +45% from trough
Consistent (wheat <2.5mt/mo vs 6.3mt y/y) but swamped by Capesize; did not dent headline BDI
Iron ore softened toward CNY 710 but Capesize freight kept rising; 30-day bearish implication did not materialize
rows.grade: Not falsified on medium-term, wrong on 30-day

rows.claim: SmartShipbroking (31 Aug): prompt strength real, fwd cautious
rows.outcome: Prompt strength confirmed (+13.9%); forward-caution untestable within window (BDI still rising to 9 Sep)

blocks.text: **Bottom line.** The consensus 'no-correction' call was correct and the highest-conviction claim (Breakwave, 18 August) was the most accurate in substance, though it understated the rally's intensity. The principal August error was the model-driven bearish-momentum call (Signal forward balance) that predicted Capesize easing into September; realized C3 and C5 strengthened to multi-year highs. The disagreement over sustainability (Xinde, Breakwave's China caveat) did not translate into lower freight within the 30-day window, and the residual risk there remains a medium-term, not a near-term, issue.

Absent a resolution to these structural geopolitical parameters, a meaningful downward correction in rates appears unlikely... we anticipate an uneventful conclusion to the summer trading period, with expectations for renewed market volatility and increased cargo flows as the industry transitions into the peak autumn and winter seasons.

# Dry Bulk Shipping 

# Bi-Weekly Industry Report  August 4, 2026 

• Dry Bulk Rate Volatility Collapses as Spot Rates Remain High – The dry bulk market continues to trade at historically elevated levels with no immediate signs of a correction, while freight rate volatility has collapsed to multi-year lows. Current spot rate strength is primarily sustained by structural vessel supply constraints, driven by ongoing geopolitical disruptions and an intensive global drydocking schedule. However, downside risks are accumulating as weakening demand for iron ore in China, the sector's primary trading commodity, threatens to disrupt the market balance. Because freight rates are fundamentally demand-driven and supply-enabled, the absence of sustained demand growth is gradually tilting the medium-term outlook. While pinpointing the exact catalyst for a market correction remains challenging, investors should look past the current period of price stability, as macroeconomic fundamentals will ultimately drive medium-term freight dynamics. However, shipowners have been riding a very strong market for multiple years in a row and thus maintain extremely healthy cash balances to weather a potential storm, unlike the 2010’ crisis when major companies where forced to reorganize. 

• Iron Ore Prices Drop to 2-Year Lows – Iron ore prices have retraced to the lower bound of their $90/t to $100/t range, hovering near two-year lows due to subdued Chinese steel demand and elevated portside inventories. While first-half imports remained resilient, sustaining this momentum through the second half appears unlikely without a substantial macroeconomic stimulus package from China. Concurrently, a five-year trend of high inflation, elevated fuel costs, and historically steep freight rates has driven miners' breakeven thresholds significantly above the previous decade averages, threatening the net profitability of several major Atlantic-basin producers once overhead is factored in. Consequently, prices are projected to drift lower in the near term, likely triggering production curtailments that will possibly contract the global seaborne iron ore trade for the remainder of the year. 

• Our Long-term View – The last few years have been characterized by increased geopolitical uncertainty. Going forward, we expect such events to continue to affect global trade and have a meaningful impact on effective vessel supply. Combined with the potential for a multi-year cyclical rebound in China’s economic activity following the recent economic turmoil, dry bulk shipping should experience higher volatility on top of a secular tightness driven by stable bulk commodity demand and rather steady but elevated fleet growth.

> Breakwave Advisors Research

**China’s steel demand remains under pressure, iron ore inventories at Chinese ports are elevated, and netbacks for Atlantic iron ore producers have fallen to their lowest level in eight years. Yet on the other side of the market, Capesize vessels have averaged more than $30,000 per day so far in 2026, nearly 80% higher than a year ago. Even more unusually, this strength has come with realized dry bulk volatility falling to at least a seven-year low.**

This is one of the most striking contradictions in today’s dry bulk market.

In its August 18 _Bi-Weekly Dry Bulk Report_, Breakwave Advisors described the current environment as “Steady As She Goes.” According to the firm, realized volatility across dry bulk has declined to at least a seven-year low even as shipowners continue to earn some of the strongest absolute daily rates seen in decades.

Part of the explanation is technical. With freight rates already sitting at elevated levels, the same absolute daily move translates into a smaller percentage change. The traditional summer slowdown has also reduced trading activity and compressed short-term volatility.

But the more important explanation lies deeper in the supply side of the freight market.

Breakwave argues that persistent geopolitical disruption across the Black Sea, Red Sea, Arabian waters and Baltic region continues to reduce vessel efficiency. As long as those structural disruptions remain in place, the conditions for a major downward correction in dry bulk freight rates remain limited.

The numbers underline just how strong the market has been.

According to the fundamentals data accompanying Breakwave’s report, the Baltic Dry Index has averaged around 2,452 points so far in 2026, up 73% year on year. Average Capesize spot earnings have reached $31,063 per day, up 77.8%, while Panamax earnings have averaged around $17,808 per day, an increase of 52%.

Separate figures cited from Xclusiv Shipbrokers point in the same direction. During the first seven months of 2026, average Capesize 5TC earnings stood at roughly $30,400 per day, compared with just $16,800 per day during the same period last year — an increase of around 81%. Rates reached $46,538 per day at the end of May and were still around $35,457 per day at the end of July.

This has therefore not been a short-lived freight spike.

The question is why Capesize earnings have remained so strong when global steel demand — and Chinese steel demand in particular — is far from booming.

### Weak Chinese steel demand does not necessarily mean weak seaborne demand

For decades, the dry bulk market has been heavily dependent on China. Iron ore, coal, bauxite, grain and a wide range of minor bulks moving into the country form the backbone of global dry bulk demand.

As a result, weaker Chinese property activity, steel production or industrial growth has traditionally been interpreted as negative for dry bulk shipping.

The relationship is now becoming more complicated.

Research published by Ocean Analytics through Breakwave on August 21 showed that China’s industrial output grew 4.5% year on year in July, below expectations, while fixed-asset investment remained weak and the property sector continued to struggle.

From a macroeconomic perspective, this hardly points to a strong commodity-demand cycle.

Yet according to Signal Ocean data cited in the same analysis, seaborne dry bulk volumes destined for China still increased 4.1% year on year during the first half of 2026 and were also nearly 2% above the same period in 2024.

China continues to account for roughly 40% of global seaborne dry bulk demand.

Breakwave therefore argues that Chinese GDP growth has become an increasingly imperfect leading indicator for the country’s dry bulk imports.

Iron ore offers the clearest example.

Chinese crude steel production has been weaker than last year, yet iron ore imports have not contracted in parallel. Earlier Breakwave research showed that China imported 112.69 million tonnes of iron ore in June, up 6.4% year on year, while imports during the first half of 2026 reached 628.87 million tonnes, an increase of 6.3%.

At the same time, a significant portion of these imports has accumulated in inventories rather than being immediately absorbed by steel production. By the end of July, Chinese port iron ore inventories had risen to around 174 million tonnes, more than 22% above the level a year earlier, while crude steel production remained roughly 3% lower year on year.

Week 35 tracks 164 freight assessments across six shipping sectors with a three-week AI outlook. Gulf tanker markets remain elevated but increasingly route-specific, East-of-Suez CPP stays firm, dry bulk has strengthened prompt, while gas and container markets continue to show a clear split between spot and period signals.

**Freight Market Outlook - Week 35 (2026)**

**Published: 31 August 2026**

**Current market observation: 28 August 2026**

**Three-week forecast horizon: 4–18 September 2026**

Week 35 brings another **164-route cross-sector view**, but the key message this week is not simply whether freight is rising or falling.

It is **where the strength sits, how long it may last, and which routes are already moving differently from their wider sector**.

That divergence is especially clear in tankers, while dry bulk has strengthened in the prompt market and gas continues to show a sizeable gap between spot and period employment.

**Crude & DPP Tankers: strong market, but route selection is everything**

Hormuz disruption continues to keep Gulf risk elevated, but Week 35 tanker performance is increasingly split. **MEG–Asia VLCC trades remain very strong**, while Atlantic VLCC and several Suezmax routes have corrected.

The report’s expert note therefore puts greater emphasis on vessel positioning and route selection than on headline tanker strength alone.

The numbers illustrate that difference. The c.2010-built **VLCC Average TCE** is around **$221,000/day**, with the model moving to roughly **$234,000/day, $295,000/day and $288,000/day** over the forward window. Meanwhile,

Suezmax average earnings have corrected to about **$165,000/day**, but recover progressively toward approximately **$227,000/day by Week +3**.

The clearest forward signal, however, is **Aframax**. Average TCE has dropped to around **$86,000/day**, but the model rebuilds earnings toward **$123,000/day by Week +3**.

TD25 shows a similar recovery pattern.

**Shipbroker view:** tanker freight remains highly rewarding, but fixing strategy matters. Owners should not assume every crude route will follow the Gulf headline higher; charterers, meanwhile, may find the better opportunities on routes where the prompt correction has run ahead of the wider fundamentals.

**Product & CPP Tankers: firm East of Suez, recovery opportunities in the Atlantic**

CPP remains highly regional. East-of-Suez LR demand is stronger than Atlantic MR prompt markets, with changing Asia-to-Africa diesel flows adding support to long-haul clean-product employment.

**TC1 ME Gulf–Japan** is currently around **WS 541** and moves higher initially before easing later. **TC5 ME–Japan** is even stronger near **WS 577**, with the model showing further near-term upside before some normalisation in the outer week.

The Atlantic offers a different opportunity. **Rotterdam–New York**, **Augusta–Lavera** and **Houston–Amsterdam** are softer prompt, but their forecast curves show meaningful recovery potential later in the window.

**Shipbroker view:** this is not a market to trade from an average CPP headline. Owners need to distinguish between prompt Atlantic weakness and stronger eastern fundamentals; charterers should equally recognise that some currently soft Atlantic routes may become more expensive if the forecast recovery develops.

**Chemical & Vegetable Oils: supported, but not a breakout**

Palm-oil demand remains supported by Indian festival buying, while Malaysian exports have been healthy. At the same time, higher production and inventories keep physical supply comfortable and limit the case for a sustained freight rally.

**Port Kelang–Rotterdam** holds around **$30,000/day**, firms marginally in Week +1, then eases toward approximately **$28,200/day by Week +3**.

The route therefore remains workable, but the forward profile favours disciplined fixing rather than chasing the prompt market.

**Gas Carriers: period cover remains the stronger story**

Gas shipping continues to show a pronounced **spot-versus-period split**. LNG spot remains weak, LPG spot has softened, while longer-duration VLGC and LPG employment is considerably more resilient.

The **160k CBM LNG spot rate** is only around **$16,250/day**, while the smaller 145k CBM benchmark remains around **$4,500/day**. By contrast, the **84k CBM VLGC one-year TC** holds near **$70,000/day** throughout the forecast horizon.

BLPG3 Houston–Chiba has eased to around **$267/tonne**, while Ras Tanura–Chiba VLGC TCE briefly firms before softening later.

The full analysis is in the report. Summary:

**August 2026 forecasts (30-day horizon) — consensus vs. disagreement**
- **Consensus (high conviction):** no major downward correction, Capesize-led strength sustained by vessel-supply tightness. Breakwave (4 & 18 Aug), BIMCO SMOO, and late-August broker notes were aligned.
- **Disagreement:** (1) Signal Group's supply/demand forward-balance model predicted C3/C5 supply surplus to widen into early September (easing) — the explicit bearish near-term call; (2) Xinde and Breakwave's own China-iron-ore caveat questioned sustainability; (3) no one forecast the breakout magnitude.

**Testing against September data (to 9 Sep)**
- BDI: 2,815 (18 Aug) → 3,620 (9 Sep), +28.6%; first week of September alone +13.9% to a near-5-year high (3,628 on 4 Sep); BCI +20.4% to 6,427.
- **Breakwave "no-correction"** — vindicated (high-conviction claim was right in substance, though "uneventful summer" understated the rally).
- **Signal model (easing into September)** — wrong direction; C3 hit a multi-year high at $41.55/mt and C5 strengthened to high-$18s.
- **Xinde/BIMCO sustainability skepticism** — not falsified medium-term, but the 30-day bearish implication did not materialize; Black Sea grains weakness (Xclusiv) was segment-correct but swamped by Capesize strength.

Sources: OilPriceAPI Baltic reprints [1][2], Breakwave Aug 4 [3] and Aug 18 [4] reports, Signal Week 31/32 forward balances [5][6], Xinde [8], BIMCO [9], SmartShipbroking Week 35 [10], Baird Baltic close [11].
